summary:
Pennsylvania's law operates inside the United States framework, which governs passports, visas, entry screening, federal custody and federally funded programmes; those national rules sit above the state layer and are not restated here. An independent anti-trans legal-risk assessment placed Pennsylvania in its low-risk tier in a July 2026 update, the category covering states that largely refrain from targeting trans adults without extending them specific protection.

Statewide discrimination protection is explicit. Since June 2023 discrimination on the basis of gender identity has been banned across Pennsylvania, with sexual orientation covered from the same date, and municipalities including Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Allentown, Erie and Reading maintain their own bans. The Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission has interpreted the Human Relations Act's prohibition on sex discrimination to cover gender identity since August 2018, investigating complaints and awarding remedies that include stop orders, training and economic damages. Legally binding regulations signed in December 2022 define sex to include gender identity. State employees have held executive-order protection since 2003 and state contractors since 7 April 2016. A bill to write gender identity and sexual orientation protection into statute, House Bill 300, passed the House 102-98 in April 2023 and awaits a Senate vote, so the current statewide guarantee rests on commission interpretation and regulation rather than legislation.

State identity documents are comparatively open. Since August 2016 a transgender person can change the gender on a Pennsylvania birth certificate on a physician's note of appropriate clinical treatment, with no requirement for surgery and a parental request required below age 18; birth certificates carry no X option. Driver's licences and state IDs have offered X alongside M and F since 23 July 2020.

Philadelphia has built a local layer on top of the state rules. Ordinances adopted in November 2019 bar youth-serving organisations from discriminating against trans, nonbinary and gender-nonconforming youth, require at least one gender-neutral bathroom in every city-owned building, and confirm that the Fair Practice Ordinance protects nonbinary and gender-fluid people; in December 2021 X was added alongside male and female in all virtual public schools. On 17 October 2023 Mayor Jim Kenney declared Philadelphia a sanctuary for gender-affirming care by executive order, prohibiting the use of city resources to investigate or punish in-state or out-of-state residents seeking such care in the city, deprioritising enforcement of any future state or federal restriction, and shielding travellers from out-of-state enforcement.

Gender-affirming surgery is lawful in Pennsylvania, and no statewide prohibition on gender-affirming care for adults appears in the sources reviewed.

Violence motivated by anti-LGBTQ bias sits outside the state hate-crime statute. A 2002 hate-crime law covering LGBTQ people was struck down in 2008 on the constitutional ground that its content had been inserted into an agricultural terrorism bill; bills to reinstate it have never left committee, leaving no statewide hate-crime provision that reaches anti-LGBTQ violence. In April 2021 a Pittsburgh mayoral proposal sought a city ordinance explicitly naming gender identity; no enactment followed.

Restrictions on transgender participation in sport have moved through the legislature without becoming law. A June 2022 bill that would have required public K-12 schools and colleges to designate sports as male, female or coed, with female-designated teams restricted to athletes assigned female at birth, passed both chambers but was vetoed on 11 July 2022 by Governor Tom Wolf. On 6 May 2025 the Senate approved Senate Bill 9, the Save Women's Sports Act, reserving women's teams for "biological females" in K-12 and collegiate sport, and sent it to the House. On 22 April 2026 the Senate passed Senate Bill 1293 under the same title; Governor Josh Shapiro called supportive lawmakers "extremists", and it was unclear whether the House would take the bill up. All of these measures concern youth school sport rather than transgender adults or public facility access.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity is legal in Pennsylvania. The sodomy statute was held unconstitutional by the state Supreme Court in the 1980 ruling Commonwealth v. Bonadio on equal protection grounds, and the remaining sodomy laws were repealed in 1995. Marriage between two people of the same sex has been recognised statewide since Whitewood v. Wolf struck down the statutory ban on 20 May 2014; before that ruling the state recognised no marriages, civil unions or domestic partnerships. Philadelphia offers life partnerships for long-term committed couples with a city nexus, Pittsburgh provides domestic partnerships, and Luzerne County defines domestic partnership as between people of the same gender.
tangentialFactors:
Older morality statutes on the books retain reach. In December 2021 an 81-year-old man was jailed for nearly two years without trial under an archaic sexual deviant law over alleged non-consensual oral sex in a nursing home.

Obscenity law has been pruned unevenly. Upper Darby's 1987 ordinance defining sexual conduct to include homosexuality was repealed in full after arguments that public displays could render even a Pride parade obscene. Two General Assembly votes in May 2021 to remove acts of homosexuality from state law 18 PA 5903 failed; in July 2022 the General Assembly unanimously passed repeal of the two-word references to homosexuality in the criminal code, which Governor Tom Wolf signed effective immediately.

In July 2026 the Governor signed Senate Bill 45, repealing a 1982 law that allowed felony rather than misdemeanor charges for people with HIV engaged in prostitution.

A 2020 Omnibus Budget Appropriations Bill added a prohibition on LGBT pride flags and cannabis flags flying at the General Assembly.
localsOnly:
Conversion therapy on minors is banned by municipal ordinance rather than state law, covering Pittsburgh, where it passed on 14 December 2016 and took effect 1 January 2017, along with Philadelphia, Allentown, Reading, Doylestown, State College, Yardley, Bellefonte, Bethlehem, Newtown Township and York. Five health boards adopted a ban in May 2024 applying to statewide healthcare policies, and an August 2022 executive order bars state government funding for conversion therapy. Statewide bills, including one introduced in April 2015 with 20 sponsors, died without action.

Parentage and adoption rules have been settled largely by the courts. In March 2025 the state Supreme Court held that same-sex couples carry the same legal parentage obligations for children conceived through IVF as heterosexual couples where an established household agreement exists, regardless of marital status. A single person may adopt without regard to sexual orientation, stepchild adoption by a same-sex partner was barred until a 6-0 Supreme Court ruling in 2002 established the right, and no statute prohibits joint adoption by a same-sex couple.

In October 2024 a district court ruled that Mt. Lebanon School District must allow parents to opt their children out of lessons or activities about transgender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
The House prospects of Senate Bill 1293 were not stated at the time of reporting, and Senate Bill 9 has sat in the House since 6 May 2025 with no recorded action.

House Bill 300 has passed only the House and awaits a Senate vote; whether the legislature will convert the commission's interpretation and the December 2022 regulations into statute is unresolved.

No reinstatement of the struck-down hate-crime provision has been sourced beyond committee referral, and the April 2021 Pittsburgh measure remained a mayoral proposal rather than an enacted ordinance.
